title: Why String Changed Everything
description: The oldest cord, Ötzi's bindings, and where plant and animal fibre hides
tryIt: Try the Army's three-step test on three dead plant fibres from your garden: pull a length, roll and twist it, then tie an overhand knot and tighten it gently.

concepts.title: How it works: the oldest string
In the field: where fibre hides
concepts.contentHtml:
You do not need a shop to find cordage; you need to know where fibre hides. In plants it is mostly in the bast, the fibrous layer of the inner bark, which eventually hardens to form bark.1 In animals it is in tendons and hide.

  1. Raid what you carry. The Army's survival manual, FM 21-76, points out that a cotton web belt becomes far more useful unravelled:2 the string serves as fishing line, sewing thread or lashing.
  2. Look for bast. The manual names the inner bark of linden (lime), elm, hickory, white oak, mulberry, chestnut and red and white cedar. Bast comes away most easily in early spring as the sap rises, and the best harvest runs from early spring to early summer.3
  3. Beat it and soak it. Beating the bark helps free the fibres, and soaking them in water, called retting, separates and softens them.
  4. Test before you trust. Pull a length to test its strength. Twist it between your fingers and roll the fibres together. If it survives, tie an overhand knot and tighten it gently. If the knot holds, the material is usable.4
  5. Sinew for small jobs. Dry the tendons of large game, smash them into fibres, then moisten and twist them into a strand. Moist sinew is sticky and hardens as it dries, so small lashings need no knots.5
  6. Rawhide for big ones. Cut dry hide into strips about 6 mm wide, soak them for 2 to 4 hours, then stretch them on wet; they dry strong and durable.
Safety On a camping trip, follow Leave No Trace rather than the survival manual: leave rocks, plants and other natural objects as you find them,6 and never strip bark from a living tree. Practise with dead stems you are allowed to collect, or with garden raffia. Wear gloves for nettles, wash your hands after handling plant sap, and only use hide or sinew from animals that were obtained legally.

concepts.title: Myth check: string, Neanderthals and a grass cape
concepts.contentHtml:
Two stories about early string get repeated far more often than they deserve.

Myth String is a late invention of modern humans; Neanderthals were too simple to make it.
Reality The Abri du Maras cord is the oldest direct evidence of fibre technology yet found,1 and Neanderthals made it. Its makers had to know which trees to strip, when the bast would come away and how to ret it. Real cord fragments were otherwise much younger: twisted fibres about 19,000 years old from Ohalo II, and remnants of a 6-ply cord about 17,000 years old from Lascaux.2
Myth Ötzi wore a cape of woven grass.
Reality Remnants of a mat woven from alpine swamp grass were found at the site and were first read as a cape. The museum that cares for him now calls that interpretation highly debatable: it was more likely a mat to keep off the rain, or part of a backpack.3 His clothing was leather, hide and braided grass, with no wool or woven textile found at all.

Wait, really? String may be older still. Shell beads from Cueva Antón are at least 115,000 years old,4 and if they were strung they are the earliest possible hint of fibre technology, though sinew or a leather thong would have done the job too. And string-hungry projects need a lot of it: in a study of the Maya, Chahine found that a maguey bag just 1.3 feet in size took more than 400 metres of cordage.5 Once people could make string, they could make bags, nets, snares and mats, and none of those survive well in the ground. That is why one archaeologist, Hurcombe, called perishable things the missing majority.

title: Making Cord from Plants
description: Why twisted fibres hold, the reverse wrap, and nettle cloth fit for a rich grave
tryIt: With garden raffia or strips of newspaper, make a reverse-wrap bracelet: twist the middle until a loop forms, twist and swap the strands, and finish with an overhand knot.

concepts.title: How it works: why a twist makes rope strong
In the field: the reverse wrap
Myth check: nettle cloth and stringy plants
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Nettle cloth was a poor person's substitute for flax.
Reality In 1861 or 1862 a cloth was found wrapped around cremated remains inside a bronze urn in the Lusehøj burial mound at Voldtofte, one of the richest Bronze Age graves in Denmark. It is about 2,800 years old, a dense, even weave of yarn 0.3 to 0.5 mm thick. A 2012 study proved it is made of nettle, and strontium isotopes showed the nettles did not grow in Denmark:1 the fibre was imported, most probably from the Kärnten-Steiermark region of Austria, where flax was already grown. The researchers concluded that nettle cloth was neither a lesser substitute for flax nor a random choice.2
Myth Any long, stringy plant will make good cord.
Reality Fibres differ enormously. Henequen is only about two-thirds as strong as abaca, and coir, from coconut husks, makes rope about one-fourth the strength of hemp, although it is light enough to float.3 That is why the survival manual insists on the pull, roll and knot test before you trust anything you have twisted.

Wait, really? Telling nettle from flax is hard, and ancient cloth has often been called flax after only superficial microscopic examinations.4 The Lusehøj team used polarised light to read which way the tiny fibrils inside each fibre spiral, and looked for calcium oxalate crystals; the two together proved nettle. Nettle never quite vanished from Europe's wardrobe, either: in Britain its bast was still being made into cloth until about 1860,5 when cheaper imports took over.

title: Five Knots Worth Knowing
description: Reef, bowline, clove hitch, sheet bend and taut-line hitch: what each is for and how it fails
tryIt: Tie a reef knot and a granny knot in two shoelaces, pull each one hard, and see which one slips.

concepts.title: How it works: why a knot holds
In the field: five knots and how they fail
concepts.contentHtml:
Five knots cover most camp jobs. For each one, learn what it is for and how it lets go.

  1. Reef knot: for binding. Left over right and under, then right over left and under. Use it to tie up a bundle or a bandage with the two ends of one cord. It fails if the ropes are wet or of different sizes.1
  2. Bowline: a loop that keeps its size. Form a small loop in the standing part, pass the end up through it, round behind the standing part and back down through the loop. The Army calls it the best knot for forming a single loop that will not tighten or slip under strain,2 and uses it for lowering people and gear.
  3. Clove hitch: rope to post. Pass the rope round the pole, cross the standing part, make a second turn and pass the end under the last turn.3 It starts and finishes lashings. If the pull will not be constant, the Army adds another round under the centre of the hitch.
  4. Sheet bend: joining unequal ropes. Make a bight in the thicker rope, pass the thinner end up through it, round the whole bight and under its own standing part. It draws tight under load but can loosen or slip when the lines go slack;4 doubling the turn makes it more secure.
  5. Taut-line hitch: the adjustable guy line. Pass the end round the tent stake, then over and round the standing part and back through the loop; go round the standing part inside the loop again, closer to the stake; finish with a half hitch round the standing part outside the loop. Slide it to tighten or loosen the line.
Safety These are camp knots, not life-support. Climbing, abseiling and rescue need training and proper equipment. The Army warns that human life should never be entrusted to one hook knot, the blackwall hitch,5 which holds only under constant strain: a reminder that some knots let go when the load changes. Stand clear of the line of a loaded rope in case it parts and whips back.

concepts.title: Myth check: the reef knot's reputation
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The reef knot is the all-purpose way to join two ropes.
Reality Old manuals oversold it. The 1911 Boy Scouts Handbook called it the commonest knot for tying two ropes together1 and said it never slips or jams, and Verrill called the square knot the best all-around knot known. Yet Verrill himself warned that it is unreliable for joining ropes of unequal size,2 which will frequently slip and sooner or later pull apart, and the Army's rigging manual says it will not hold if the ropes are wet or of different sizes. Use it for binding; use a sheet bend to join.
Myth It does not matter which way round you cross the ends.
Reality Cross the same way twice and you get the granny, which the 1911 handbook says is always bad and Verrill called a most useless, bothersome and deceptive makeshift.3 The Army's rule is simple: it makes no difference which way you tie the first crossing, as long as the second is tied opposite to the first.4

Wait, really? The MIT team worked out their stability rules partly by comparing exactly these look-alikes: the granny, reef, thief and grief knots.5 Knot skill was once the ticket into scouting itself. To become a Tenderfoot in 1911, a boy had to tie four knots from a list6 that included the reef, the sheet bend, the bowline and the clove hitch.

title: Lashings and Rope Machines
description: Levers, pulleys and mechanical advantage, the square lashing and a tripod that needs no guy lines
tryIt: Lash three garden canes into a small tripod with a figure-of-eight lashing, stand it up and hang a bag of pegs from the top.

concepts.title: How it works: levers, pulleys and mechanical advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
The log you need for a ridgepole weighs more than you do. You cannot lift it. But you have rope, a few poles and physics, which is how people have always moved things too heavy for muscle alone.

The Army's rigging manual starts from a simple idea: to move a load heavier than you can manage, use a machine that multiplies the force you apply. A lever, a screw and a tackle all work the same way, and the mechanical advantage of a machine is the amount by which it multiplies the force applied to it.1 Push down 10 pounds on one end of a lever and raise a 100-pound load on the other, and the lever has a mechanical advantage of 10.2

Rope gives you the tackle: an assembly of ropes and blocks, frames holding one or more pulleys called sheaves. A block fixed to a support can change the direction of your pull, and blocks used only to change direction do not affect the mechanical advantage.3 A block that travels with the load is different. For a simple tackle, count the lines supporting the travelling block: the mechanical advantage is the same as the number of lines supporting the load.4 Hook the pull of one 4:1 tackle onto the travelling block of another and the advantages multiply, to 16:1.5

Nothing is free, though. With a 3:1 tackle you haul three metres of rope to raise the load one metre: the work you put in is the work you get out, minus friction.

concepts.title: In the field: the square lashing and the tripod
concepts.contentHtml:
A lashing binds poles together. The Scout Association calls the square lashing the most widely used lashing for securing one spar to another where they cross at an angle,1 especially to stop them sliding over each other. Learn the clove hitch first: it starts and finishes almost every lashing.

  1. Start with a clove hitch on one spar, close to the crossing.
  2. Wrap. Make at least four complete turns around both spars,2 keeping each one tight and tidy.
  3. Frap. Take at least two frapping turns between the spars, round the wrapping turns, to draw the joint together. The Scouts suggest one person pulling hard on the end while a partner keeps the corners tight.
  4. Finish with another clove hitch on the opposite spar to the one you started on.
  5. For a tripod, lay three similar spars side by side, tie a clove hitch on an outer one, then weave over the middle spar, under and round the far one, back under the middle and over and round the first, for eight turns; finish with a clove hitch. Keep it slightly loose so the legs can open. A tripod is stable and needs no guy lines, but it can only move a load up and down.
  6. Stand it up with each leg the same distance from the others, a spread of between one-half and two-thirds of the leg length.3
Safety The Scouts' rules: be able to tie lashings confidently before you build, start small, carry out a risk assessment, and make sure a structure is safe and properly anchored before anyone uses it.4 Strip bark from poles and avoid brittle woods like willow and poplar.5 For anchors, the Army warns against dead or rotten trees and stumps, which can snap suddenly under strain. Never stand under a raised load.

concepts.title: Myth check: free strength
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Any pulley makes a load easier to lift.
Reality A single fixed pulley only changes the direction of your pull. Hanging a block from a branch lets you pull down instead of up, which helps, but you still pull the full weight. Advantage comes only from lines that support a block moving with the load.
Myth Add enough pulleys and anyone can lift anything.
Reality Every sheave adds friction: the sheave rolling on its pin, the rope rubbing against the sheave and ropes rubbing together. The Army expects each sheave to create a resistance equal to about 10 per cent of the weight of the load.1 In its worked example, a 5,000-pound load on a 4:1 tackle with four sheaves picks up 2,000 pounds of friction, so the pull needed is 1,750 pounds instead of the ideal 1,250.2 Twisted ropes make things worse, adding friction and chafing and risking jammed blocks.3

Wait, really? Direction matters for people too. The Army reckons men of average weight can pull about 100 pounds each on a vertical line but only about 60 pounds on a horizontal one,4 yet more people can crowd onto a single horizontal line along the ground than onto a vertical one. And rope and poles are ancient partners: Ötzi's backpack frame, a U-shaped hazel rod about 2 metres long with two narrow wooden boards, was probably tied together with string.5

title: Stone Tools
description: Conchoidal fracture and the cone of percussion, Oldowan to Acheulean, and how sharp a flake can be
tryIt: Where flint is common and you are allowed to look, find a naturally broken flint pebble, spot its smooth, rippled conchoidal surface, then leave it where it lies.

concepts.title: How it works: the cone of percussion
concepts.contentHtml:
Your knife is gone, lost in the river. On the gravel bar at your feet lie hundreds of grey, glassy pebbles. Somewhere among them is the oldest cutting technology on Earth, waiting to be let out with one well-aimed blow.

Not every stone will do. Chipped stone tools can be made only from a few rocks composed largely of silica.1 Flint and chert are cryptocrystalline, built of tiny needlelike quartz crystals,2 and obsidian is volcanic glass. With no large crystals to steer a crack, they break much like common glass, producing conchoidal fractures, with curved, shell-like surfaces, because the energy of a blow spreads out radially from the point of contact.3

Fracture mechanics explains the shape. Strike a core and the impact starts a Hertzian cone, or cone crack, at the point of percussion, the same crack a hard object makes when pressed onto a brittle solid: in three dimensions, a truncated cone below the impact surface.4 Its size varies with the hammer and the force, but its angle stays constant for a given material, about 136 degrees in soda-lime glass.5 Once the crack reaches a certain length it stops following the cone and runs almost parallel to the core's surface.6 That peels off a flake, and the start of the cone survives on it as the bulb of percussion.

Read a flake like a story. The flat surface where it was struck is the platform. A hard hammer often leaves a crushed point of percussion there and a swelling below it, the bulb, sometimes with a small chip knocked off it called an eraillure scar.7 Ripples spreading from the bulb record the path of the crack.

concepts.title: In the field: from Oldowan to a knife edge
concepts.contentHtml:
Stone toolmaking is at least 2.6 million years old.1 The oldest widely known kit, the Oldowan, has three parts: hammerstones battered from use, cores with flake scars along their edges, and the sharp flakes struck from them, plus lots of debris. By about 1.76 million years ago early humans were striking really large flakes2 and shaping them further into handaxes, the hallmark of the Acheulean. Both kits were made for an immense time, ending in different places around 400,000 to 250,000 years ago.3

The steps below are how archaeologists and the Army describe the craft. Read them as history and science; if you want to try knapping, do it on a supervised course.

  1. Choose the stone. Fine-grained flint, chert or obsidian, which break like glass.
  2. Hard hammer first. Strike the core with a hammerstone near the edge of a flat platform to knock off flakes; this is the earliest and most basic technique.4
  3. Soft hammer to thin. A hammer of antler, bone or wood removes thinner, flatter flakes with a smaller platform.
  4. Pressure to sharpen. Press a pointed flaking tool of bone or antler against the edge: flakes come off the opposite side, leaving a razor-sharp edge.5
  5. Haft it. Lash the blade into a handle, as Ötzi's dagger blade was bound into its handle with sinew.
Safety Flakes are sharper than they look and fly off fast: anyone knapping wears eye protection and gloves, works outdoors and keeps onlookers back. Flint dust is a lung hazard; flint-knappers in East Anglia suffered silicosis, known as knappers' rot.6 Collecting is restricted in many places. In US national parks the rule is to leave rocks and other natural objects as you find them, and old worked flints are artefacts to photograph, not pocket.

concepts.title: Myth check: crude tools and clever apes
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Stone tools began with our own genus, Homo.
Reality Scholars long supposed so. Then in 2015 Sonia Harmand and her colleagues reported Lomekwi 3 in West Turkana, Kenya: a 3.3-million-year-old site where stone artefacts lie with Pliocene hominin fossils.1 Its knappers combined core reduction with battering, and the team named the industry the Lomekwian, which predates the Oldowan by 700,000 years.2
Myth Stone tools are crude and blunt, and a handaxe beats a flake at everything.
Reality In large experiments, Alastair Key and Stephen Lycett found simple flakes significantly more efficient than handaxes for small, precise cutting,3 while handaxes won at cutting large, resistant pieces of material. Sharpness is not the problem either. In 1982 the surgeon Bruce Buck wrote that a prismatic blade of volcanic glass is infinitely sharper than a honed steel edge;4 such blades had been used in experimental microsurgery, and in animal tests the wounds healed at least as strongly as steel-scalpel cuts. The weakness is toughness: the Army notes that stone makes an excellent puncturing tool and a good chopping tool but will not hold a fine edge.5

Wait, really? Ötzi was not a flintknapper, according to the team that studied his toolkit, but he could resharpen his tools with a medium to good level of skill,6 and wear traces show he was right-handed. His dagger blade is very small, hardly bigger than an arrowhead, perhaps because it was resharpened so often.
